analysis.one_liner: Gives federal and state enforcers more power and money to investigate police departments for patterns of misconduct.
analysis.headline: A police-accountability bill introduced with 9 cosponsors in May 2024 never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the federal government's main tool for addressing police departments with patterns of unconstitutional conduct: it would add money and staff for Justice Department investigations, require civilian oversight boards in court-enforced reform agreements, and let state attorneys general sue their own state agencies in federal court. It would also expand the law to cover prosecutors, judges, and other justice officials, and fund non-police responses like mental health crisis teams and social workers. The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of cities and states where police departments, prosecutors, or courts show patterns of unconstitutional conduct would gain stronger federal investigations, court-enforced reform agreements that include civilian oversight and non-police remedies like mental health support, and grants for alternatives to police responses. State attorneys general would gain a new power to bring federal pattern-or-practice suits against agencies in their own states, with safeguards to keep investigators independent of the agencies they are investigating. People with disabilities are specifically called out as a group whose treatment should be addressed under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Attorney General to design consent decrees — court-enforced reform agreements with police agencies — that include remedies beyond police procedures, such as mental health support and community-based restorative justice, and to seek guidance from other agencies on how well those alternatives work.

Requires that, where possible, consent decrees include a community oversight body made up of people who have never worked in law enforcement, with the authority to question the agency, obtain its documents and data, and recommend changes.

Authorizes $445 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2034 for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, with at least $100 million of that reserved each year for pattern-or-practice enforcement, plus annual reports to Congress on how the money is used.

Expands the underlying law so it covers not just law enforcement officers but also prosecutors, judges, and other government officials involved in administering justice, while protecting prosecutors' discretion to decide not to bring charges in individual cases.

Lets state attorneys general bring the same pattern-or-practice suits in federal court against agencies in their own states, with conflict-of-interest rules requiring independent investigators and an independent organization when the target is a statewide office, plus Justice Department technical assistance.

Creates a $150 million-a-year grant program for states to run their own pattern-or-practice investigations, implement reforms, and fund non-police programs such as social workers, behavioral health crisis experts, and alternatives to police enforcement of traffic rules — with repayment required if funds are diverted to ordinary police operations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $595 million a year in new spending authorizations ($445 million for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division plus $150 million in state grants) for ten years — about $5.95 billion total, subject to annual appropriations. State and local police agencies, prosecutors' offices, and courts would bear the costs of investigations, lawsuits, and court-ordered reforms.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes nearly $6 billion in new federal spending over ten years ($445 million plus $150 million per year for fiscal years 2025 through 2034), which would need annual approval from Congress.

Extending the law to prosecutors and judges raises good-faith concerns about pulling the Justice Department into the independence of courts and prosecution; the bill shields only the decision to decline charges, leaving other prosecutorial and judicial conduct open to civil suits.

The community oversight bodies must be staffed by people who have never worked in law enforcement; supporters see that as independence, but it means the people policing compliance with reform agreements would have no operational policing experience.

The bill's enforcement still depends on the willingness of future attorneys general and state officials to open investigations and file suits — it adds tools and money but does not require any investigation to be launched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability mechanisms are real: more investigators, a new avenue for state-led suits, and civilian oversight written into court-enforced reforms would give communities affected by police misconduct more recourse than they have today. The roughly $595 million annual authorization is modest by federal standards but is not guaranteed money — it must clear annual appropriations each year. The design risks are dependence on the priorities of whichever administration runs the Justice Department, and the expansion to prosecutors and judges, which reaches beyond policing into institutions where independence is a genuine value; the bill's carve-out for charging decisions blunts but does not eliminate that concern.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 22, 2024, with nine original cosponsors: eight Democrats and one independent.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local police agencies, prosecutors, and courts avoided new federal investigations, consent decrees, civilian oversight, and compliance costs; no community gained the bill's remedies because none were enacted.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Hirono, Duckworth, Wyden, Merkley, Van Hollen, Booker, Welch, Markey).

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten original sponsors were Democrats or the independent who caucuses with them; no Republican cosponsored, and because no vote was ever held, opposition was expressed only through inaction.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would expose departments to more federal and state pattern-or-practice suits, court-enforced consent decrees, and civilian oversight bodies with the power to demand documents and data. Its grant money is specifically barred from being diverted to police operations.

For the first time, prosecutors and judges would be named in the statute as subject to pattern-or-practice suits, ending their exemption; the bill offsets this by explicitly protecting a prosecutor's discretion to decline charges. The new exposure runs against public accountability interests, the carve-out preserves core prosecutorial power.

industries.industry: Community mental health and crisis-response services
industries.note: Consent decrees would be required to consider mental health and restorative-justice remedies, and state grants could fund social workers, behavioral health crisis experts, and alternatives to police traffic enforcement — new public funding flowing to these services.
